title: Exercise and Respiration
content:
# Exercise and Respiration

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Explain how exercise affects respiration rate
- Describe changes in breathing and heart rate during exercise
- Explain the switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration during intense exercise
- Understand how the body adapts to regular exercise

## Introduction

During exercise, muscles need more energy, so respiration rate increases. The body makes several adjustments to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove more carbon dioxide. Understanding these changes helps explain how exercise affects the body.

## Key Concepts

### Why Does Exercise Increase Energy Demand?

**Muscles need more ATP for:**
- Contraction (movement)
- Maintaining force
- Recovery between contractions

**More ATP needed = more respiration required**

### Changes During Exercise

| System | Change | Reason |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Breathing rate | Increases | More O₂ in, more CO₂ out |
| Breathing depth | Increases | More air per breath |
| Heart rate | Increases | Faster blood circulation |
| Stroke volume | Increases | More blood per beat |
| Blood flow to muscles | Increases | Delivers O₂ and glucose |
| Blood flow to gut | Decreases | Diverted to muscles |

### The Demand-Supply Problem

**During rest:**
- O₂ supply = O₂ demand
- Aerobic respiration only
- Steady state

**During intense exercise:**
- O₂ demand > O₂ supply
- Anaerobic respiration begins
- Lactic acid accumulates

[DIAGRAM: Graph showing oxygen supply vs demand during exercise]

### Changes to Breathing

**Ventilation rate:**
$$\text{Ventilation rate} = \text{Breathing rate} \times \text{Tidal volume}$$

| Activity | Breathing rate | Tidal volume | Ventilation rate |
|----------|---------------|--------------|------------------|
| Rest | ~15 /min | ~0.5 L | ~7.5 L/min |
| Exercise | ~40 /min | ~2.5 L | ~100 L/min |

### Changes to Heart Rate

**Cardiac output:**
$$\text{Cardiac output} = \text{Heart rate} \times \text{Stroke volume}$$

| Activity | Heart rate | Stroke volume | Cardiac output |
|----------|------------|---------------|----------------|
| Rest | ~70 bpm | ~70 mL | ~5 L/min |
| Exercise | ~180 bpm | ~120 mL | ~22 L/min |

### Blood Redistribution

**At rest vs during exercise:**

| Organ | Rest (%) | Exercise (%) |
|-------|----------|---------------|
| Muscles | 20 | 85 |
| Digestive system | 25 | 3 |
| Kidneys | 20 | 2 |
| Skin | 5 | 5 |
| Brain | 15 | 3 |
| Heart | 5 | 5 |

**Why redistribution?**
- Muscles need more oxygen and glucose
- Non-essential organs can wait
- Blood is limited resource

### Aerobic vs Anaerobic During Exercise

| Exercise intensity | Main respiration | Products |
|-------------------|------------------|----------|
| Light (walking) | Aerobic | CO₂, H₂O |
| Moderate (jogging) | Mainly aerobic | CO₂, H₂O |
| Intense (sprinting) | Both | CO₂, H₂O + lactic acid |

### The Lactate Threshold

**Definition:** The exercise intensity where lactic acid starts to accumulate

**Before threshold:**
- Aerobic respiration matches demand
- No lactic acid build-up

**Above threshold:**
- Anaerobic respiration needed
- Lactic acid accumulates
- Fatigue develops

[DIAGRAM: Graph showing lactate threshold during increasing exercise intensity]

### Effects of Lactic Acid

| Effect | Consequence |
|--------|-------------|
| Muscle pH drops | Enzyme activity decreases |
| Pain/burning | Discomfort signals |
| Reduced contraction | Muscle fatigue |
| Cramp possible | Sustained contraction |

### Recovery After Exercise

**What needs to happen:**
1. Lactic acid removed
2. Oxygen stores replenished
3. Glycogen restored
4. Heart rate returns to resting
5. Body temperature normalises

**Recovery takes time:**
- Heart and breathing rate stay elevated
- Extra oxygen consumed (EPOC)
- Lactic acid processed in liver

### Measuring Exercise Effects

**Pulse rate monitoring:**
- Measure before exercise (resting rate)
- Measure immediately after
- Measure at intervals during recovery
- Calculate recovery time

**Recovery time:**
- Fitter people recover faster
- Can be used to assess fitness

### Factors Affecting Exercise Response

| Factor | Effect on performance |
|--------|----------------------|
| Fitness level | Fitter = better response |
| Training | Improves efficiency |
| Age | Older = slower max heart rate |
| Health | Disease reduces capacity |
| Temperature | Heat increases strain |

### Adaptations to Regular Exercise

| Adaptation | Benefit |
|------------|----------|
| More mitochondria | More ATP production |
| Increased capillary density | Better O₂ delivery |
| Larger heart (athlete's heart) | Greater stroke volume |
| More myoglobin | Better O₂ storage in muscle |
| Higher lactate threshold | Exercise longer before fatigue |
| Lower resting heart rate | More efficient heart |

### VO₂ Max

**Definition:** Maximum rate of oxygen consumption during exercise

**Why it matters:**
- Indicator of aerobic fitness
- Higher = better endurance
- Trainable (can be improved)

| Fitness level | VO₂ max (mL/kg/min) |
|---------------|---------------------|
| Untrained | 30-40 |
| Average | 40-50 |
| Athletic | 50-60 |
| Elite endurance | 70-85 |

## Common Exam Questions

- Explain why breathing rate increases during exercise
- Describe what happens to heart rate during and after exercise
- Explain why anaerobic respiration occurs during intense exercise
- Describe adaptations to regular exercise

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Lactic acid causes muscle soreness days after exercise
- **Reality:** Delayed soreness is from muscle damage, not lactic acid

- **Misconception:** Anaerobic respiration only starts when aerobic stops
- **Reality:** Both can occur simultaneously during intense exercise

- **Misconception:** Breathing hard is just to get rid of CO₂
- **Reality:** It's also to get more O₂ for increased respiration

- **Misconception:** Heart rate returns to normal immediately after exercise
- **Reality:** Recovery takes time; fitter individuals recover faster

## Practice Questions

1. State two changes to the cardiovascular system during exercise. (2 marks)

2. Explain why muscles may produce lactic acid during a sprint. (3 marks)

3. A student measured their pulse before and after exercise. Their resting pulse was 72 bpm and immediately after exercise was 156 bpm. Calculate the percentage increase. (2 marks)

4. Explain why breathing rate remains elevated for some time after exercise stops. (3 marks)

5. Describe how regular exercise training leads to adaptations in muscle cells. (4 marks)

6. Compare the changes in breathing and circulation during moderate exercise and intense exercise. Explain why these differences occur. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Cardiac output | Volume of blood pumped by heart per minute |
| Stroke volume | Volume of blood pumped per heartbeat |
| Ventilation rate | Volume of air breathed per minute |
| Lactate threshold | Exercise intensity where lactic acid accumulates |
| EPOC | Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption |
| VO₂ max | Maximum oxygen consumption rate |
| Recovery time | Time for heart rate to return to resting |

## Summary

- Exercise increases energy demand in muscles
- Heart rate, breathing rate, and depth all increase
- Blood is redirected from gut to muscles
- Above lactate threshold, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid
- Recovery requires extra oxygen to remove lactic acid
- Regular training causes adaptations: more mitochondria, lower resting heart rate, higher VO₂ max
- Fitter individuals recover faster after exercise
